deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated parts: an error-theory / least-squares note at the top, and number-theoretic scratch work in Z[i] and Q(i, sqrt79) at the bottom.

(A) Propagation of error. Let x, y, z, ... be mutually independent quantities. Each has most probable value 0, the same precision, and 'possible error' ±1 for a fixed probability (a probable error). For T = αx + βy + γz + ..., the most probable value of T is 0. Its possible error at the same probability is ±sqrt(α² + β² + γ² + ...). Gauss stresses that this holds only insofar as x, y, z are fully independent. In modern terms: if Var(x_j) = σ², then Var(Σα_j x_j) = σ² Σα_j², and fixed-probability error bounds scale with the standard deviation.

(B) Two-row reduction of a weighted sum of squares, eliminating x from one form. Let T = Ax + By + Cz + ... and t = ax + by + cz + ..., with weights M and m (inverse error scales). The goal is to write
  M²T² + m²t² = M'²T'² + m'²t'²,
where t' = b'y + c'z + ... contains no x. Gauss marks the missing x term with '*'. In the second line he omits the square on M'M'(A'x + ...); this is a slip.

Gauss's recipe:
- f = a/A, g = M/m, h = f/g, tan φ = h, i = g/h;
- T' = t + iT, t' = t − fT;
- M' = m sin φ, m' = m cos φ.

Verification (mine):
- The x-coefficient of t' is a − (a/A)A = 0.
- Expanding, M'²T'² + m'²t'² = m²[t² + 2tT(i sin²φ − f cos²φ) + T²(i² sin²φ + f² cos²φ)].
- The cross term vanishes because i tan²φ = (g/h)h² = gh = f.
- Since i = g/h and f = gh, the T² coefficient is g²(sin²φ/h² + h² cos²φ) = g²(cos²φ + sin²φ) = g². Hence m²g²T² = M²T².
- So the identity holds.

In terms of the weighted rows u = MT and v = mt one gets M'T' = cos φ·u + sin φ·v and m't' = −sin φ·u + cos φ·v, with tan φ = ma/(MA). This is exactly a plane (Givens-type) rotation of the two weighted observation rows, chosen to annihilate the x-coefficient of the second row. It is the elementary step for re-triangularizing a least-squares system when a new equation is added, or for eliminating an unknown while keeping the form a weighted sum of squares.

(C) Number-theoretic scratch, related to the next page (73, sqrt79 = 8.8882, (33 − sqrt(−79))/(3 + 8 sqrt(−1)), (3 − 7i)² = −40 − 42i, 117 − 336 = −219, −438).
- 73 = 3² + 8² = N(3 + 8i), a Gaussian prime.
- The key relation, verified via the next page, is (−3 + 7i)² + 79 = 39 − 42i = (3 + 8i)(−3 − 6i). So −3 + 7i is a square root of −79 modulo π = 3 + 8i.
- Checked in F_73, where i ≡ 27: −3 + 7·27 = 186 ≡ 40 ≡ −33, and 33² ≡ −6 ≡ −79 (mod 73). This matches the '33' on the next page.
- Hence (−3 + 7i + sqrt(−79))(−3 + 7i − sqrt(−79)) = (3 + 8i)(−3 − 6i): the splitting of π in Q(i, sqrt(−79)).
- The columns +8i, 3 + 8i, −3 − 6i, −8, −3 + 6i and 1 + 12i, −3 + 7i, 3 + 8i, −3 + 8i are trial residues and multiples in this search.
- The line '(−3 − 6i)x − 3 + 7i = sqrt79·i' with x = 2 + i is a trial linear relation. Indeed (−3 − 6i)(2 + i) − 3 + 7i = −15i − 3 + 7i = −3 − 8i = −π, written just below.
- The surd lines (−3 + 14 − 2 sqrt79, 11 − 2 sqrt79 + (13 − sqrt79)i, 7 − sqrt79, 3 − (7 − sqrt79)i over −3 − 6i, the 15s) are divisions in Q(i, sqrt79) that I cannot fully reconstruct.

From 'Br' onward:
- Gauss considers (p + q sqrt(−1))² + 79(r + s sqrt(−1))² = 1, i.e. relative-norm-1 elements of Q(i, sqrt(−79))/Q(i).
- He writes the general element p + qi + r sqrt(−79) + s sqrt79.
- He writes its norm to Q(sqrt79) as (p + s sqrt79)² + (q + r sqrt79)², with rational part pp + 79ss + qq + 79rr.
- Note (mine): with his sign of s, the Q(i)-norm of that element is (p + qi)² + 79(r − si)²; the two norms are different objects.
- Finally, x² − 3 + 8i times its conjugate gives x⁴ − 6x² + 73, the minimal polynomial of sqrt(3 ± 8i), whose norm is 73.
- 'k.', 'ku', 'W' are pen trials.
errors: In the target form Gauss writes M'M'(A'x + B'y + C'z + etc.) without the square; it must be squared (slip).

Sign convention: for the element p + q√−1 + r√−79 + s√79 the Q(i)-relative norm is (p+qi)² + 79(r − si)², not (p+qi)² + 79(r+si)². The norm to Q(√79), (p+s√79)² + (q+r√79)², is a different form. Gauss juxtaposes the two without comment (not an error, but ambiguous).
The line '(−3−6i)x − 3+7i = √79·i' with x = 2+i actually yields −3−8i (≡ 0 mod 3+8i), not √79·i literally; it is a congruence-style trial, not an equality.
The rotation (B) itself is correct; the error-propagation rule (A) is correct under independence.

results.what: Probable error of a linear combination of independent equally precise quantities: ±sqrt(α²+β²+γ²+...)
results.modern_name: Propagation of error / variance of a linear combination of independent variables
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Theoria Motus 1809; Theoria Combinationis 1821-23) and Laplace (Théorie analytique 1812)

results.what: Rewriting M²T² + m²t² as M'²T'² + m'²t'² with t' free of x via tan φ = ma/(MA), M' = m sin φ, m' = m cos φ, i.e. a plane rotation of two weighted observation rows annihilating one coefficient
results.modern_name: Givens rotation (orthogonal 2x2 rotation) for least-squares re-triangularization / updating
results.usually_credited_to: W. Givens (1954/58) for its use in triangularization; plane rotations for diagonalization go back to Jacobi (1846)

results.what: (−3+7i)² + 79 = (3+8i)(−3−6i): square root of −79 modulo the Gaussian prime 3+8i (norm 73), i.e. splitting of 3+8i in Q(i,√−79)
results.modern_name: Splitting of primes / ideal factorization in the biquadratic field Q(i, √−79); quadratic forms over Z[i]
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss's Nachlass work on biquadratic residues and forms over Gaussian integers; later Dirichlet (1840s) on forms with complex integer coefficients

results.what: Norm-1 equation (p+qi)² + 79(r+si)² = 1 and norms of elements of Q(i,√79)
results.modern_name: Relative norm / units in a biquadratic field (Pell equation over Z[i])

deep.surprise_reason: The error-propagation rule is well known to be Gauss's, and the number-theoretic scratch fits his known Nachlass work on biquadratic residues and forms over Z[i]. The one notable item is the explicit trigonometric parametrization (tan φ, M' = m sin φ, m' = m cos φ). It amounts to a Givens-type plane rotation of weighted observation rows used to eliminate an unknown while preserving a weighted sum of squares, the core of modern orthogonal least-squares updating. The algebra is elementary, and Gauss's published updating method (1823) is different. As an unpublished anticipation of the rotation idea in least squares it is a notable detail, not a major result.
